help.intro: sein (to be) and haben (to have) are the two verbs you cannot say a German sentence without. You describe yourself with sein (ich bin müde), say what you own with haben (ich habe einen Hund), and later in the course you build every past-tense sentence with one of the two (ich habe gegessen, ich bin gefahren). Both are irregular. sein is irregular through and through — bin, bist, ist, sind, seid, sind — with no pattern to lean on; haben is regular except that du hast and er hat drop the b. Learn both sets by heart now; they come up in every exercise from here to the end of the course.
help.tips[0].title: sein — six forms, no pattern
help.tips[0].text: ich bin, du bist, er/sie/es ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie/Sie sind. Note that wir and sie share sind.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: I am a student. You are nice. He is tall.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: We are from Vienna. You are tired. They are here.
help.tips[0].check.why: ihr takes seid. Watch the spelling: seit (with t) means 'since'.
help.tips[1].title: haben — regular, but two forms lose the b
help.tips[1].text: ich habe, du hast, er/sie/es hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie/Sie haben. Only hast and hat are shortened.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: I have a brother. Do you have time? She has a car.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: We are hungry. Do you have children?
help.tips[1].check.why: du drops the b: du hast. hat is for er/sie/es, habe for ich.
help.tips[2].title: haben where English says 'to be'
help.tips[2].text: German is hungry, thirsty, afraid and in a hurry with haben: Ich habe Hunger, Durst, Angst, Zeit. Age, on the other hand, uses sein: Ich bin zwanzig.
help.tips[2].trap: 'I am hungry' word-for-word (Ich bin hungrig) is understood but sounds foreign; Germans say they *have* hunger.
help.tips[2].check.why: Germans have fear, hunger and thirst: wir haben Angst.
help.tips[3].title: möchte — the polite “would like”
help.tips[3].text: möchte orders, asks and wishes without sounding blunt: Ich möchte einen Kaffee. It conjugates like a modal verb — ich möchte, du möchtest, er möchte, wir möchten, ihr möchtet, sie möchten — so ich and er share one form.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: I would like a coffee, please.
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: Would you like an ice cream too?
help.tips[3].examples[2].en: What would you like to drink?
help.tips[3].trap: English “I want” is ich will — correct, but blunt in a café. ich möchte is what people actually say when ordering.
help.tips[3].check.q: At the bakery: Ich ____ zwei Brötchen, bitte.
help.tips[3].check.why: ich takes möchte, the same form as er/sie/es.
help.remember[0]: bin-bist-ist / sind-seid-sind: chant it like a football rhythm until it needs no thought.
help.remember[1]: hast and hat have no b — the two shortest forms are the two you use most.
help.remember[2]: möchte = would like: ich möchte, du möchtest, er möchte, wir möchten, ihr möchtet, sie möchten.
help.vocab[10].en: would like (ich möchte = I would like)
help.context.en: I'm Lena and I'm a teacher. I have two children. My son is eight and my daughter is five. We also have a dog. Are you tired? – No, but I'm hungry!
help.mistakes[0].why: du hast drops the b; it is one of the two shortened forms.
help.mistakes[1].why: Hunger, thirst, fear and time are things you *have* in German.
help.mistakes[2].why: Like Hunger, Durst is a noun you have — 'durstig' is understood but not what Germans say.
help.hook: Two verbs carry half of everyday German: sein for who you are, haben for what you've got.
categories[0].label: sein (to be)
categories[1].label: haben (to have)
sentences[0].english: I am tired and am going to bed.
sentences[0].why: sein with ich is bin — its forms don't look like sein; they are learnt as a set.
sentences[1].english: Are you a student? – Yes, in Cologne.
sentences[1].why: du takes bist — the -st is the du ending; in a question the verb comes first.
sentences[2].english: My brother is twenty years old.
sentences[2].why: mein Bruder = er, and er/sie/es takes ist.
sentences[3].english: We are from Vienna, but we live in Berlin.
sentences[4].why: ihr takes seid — the one form of sein that ends in -d.
sentences[5].english: Anna and Tom are at school.
sentences[5].why: Two names = sie ('they'), and sie takes sind.
sentences[6].english: Are you Mr Müller? – Yes, that is me.
sentences[6].why: Formal Sie takes sind, and a yes/no question starts with the verb.
sentences[7].why: das Wetter = es, and er/sie/es takes ist.
sentences[8].english: Hello, I am Lena, the new colleague.
sentences[8].why: ich bin — introducing yourself always uses bin.
sentences[9].english: I have a dog and two cats.
sentences[9].why: haben with ich is habe — the regular -e ending.
sentences[10].english: Do you have time? We are going to the cinema.
sentences[10].why: du hast — haben drops the b in the du form: hast, never habst.
sentences[11].why: meine Schwester = sie, and er/sie/es is hat — again without the b.
sentences[12].english: We are hungry. Where is a restaurant?
sentences[12].why: wir haben — the plural forms keep the full stem with its b.
sentences[13].english: Do you have children? – Yes, a son.
sentences[13].why: ihr habt — the ihr ending is -t, and the question starts with the verb.
sentences[14].english: The children have the day off today.
sentences[14].why: die Kinder = sie ('they'), and sie takes haben.
sentences[15].english: Do you have a moment, Mrs Weber?
sentences[15].why: Formal Sie always takes the -en form: Haben Sie.
sentences[16].why: das Kind = es, and er/sie/es is hat — no b.
sentences[17].why: du hast — -st for du, and haben loses its b there.
sentences[18].why: mein Opa = er: hat. German has a birthday rather than 'is having' one.
sentences[19].why: ihr takes seid — sein's ihr form.
sentences[20].why: ich habe — German has fear (Angst haben) where English is afraid.
sentences[21].english: I would like a coffee, please.
sentences[21].why: ich möchte — möchte takes no extra ending with ich.
sentences[22].english: Would you like an ice cream too?
sentences[22].why: du möchtest — the du ending -st sits on möchte.
sentences[23].english: She would like a glass of water.
sentences[23].why: er/sie/es is möchte — the same form as ich, with no -t. One of möchte's surprises.
sentences[24].english: We would like two tickets to Hamburg.
sentences[24].why: wir möchten — plural subjects take the -en form.
sentences[25].english: Would you (all) like tea or coffee?
sentences[25].why: ihr möchtet — the ihr ending is -t: möchtet.
sentences[26].english: What would you like to drink?
sentences[26].why: Formal Sie takes the -en form: möchten.
